meta.name: The Ultimate Color Psychology & Cinematography Matrix - dataset
notes: All preset "grade" objects are fully resolved: every field is present, 0 or 1 means neutral.
lift/gamma/gain/offset channels are -1..1 shifts; exposure is in stops; kelvin is absolute; tint -1 (green) to +1 (magenta); contrast/saturation are multipliers.
Film stock and look grades are hand-tuned starting points, not measured emulations.
Skin line: app default is 135 degrees; standard broadcast I-line is about 123 degrees.

colorPsychology.name: Red

culturalMeanings.meaning: love, danger, stop signals, Valentine's Day

colorPsychology.cinematicUse: Used sparingly as an accent to pull the eye or signal danger, desire or violence. Heavily saturated reds clip and bleed easily on video, so most colorists protect them with Hue vs Sat.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Push Lift/Offset toward red-orange for menace. Keep red saturation below roughly 80% to avoid channel clipping. Pair with desaturated teal backgrounds so the red reads as a deliberate accent.

colorPsychology.name: Orange
colorPsychology.cinematicUse: The base of the teal and orange look: skin and fire sit in the orange range, so it is the natural counterweight to cool shadows.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Skin tones live between orange and red on the vectorscope. Move shadows toward teal and highlights toward warm orange, then use a skin-tone qualifier to keep faces from turning neon.

colorPsychology.name: Yellow
colorPsychology.cinematicUse: Warm yellow suggests sun and memory; a green-leaning yellow suggests decay, illness or paranoia. It is the brightest hue, so it draws attention at lower saturation than any other color.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Watch for yellow shifting toward green in highlights when raising Gain. Use Hue vs Hue to rotate sickly yellow-green toward warm gold when you want nostalgia rather than unease.

colorPsychology.name: Green
colorPsychology.cinematicUse: Cooler greens read as natural and calm; yellow-greens and cyan-greens feel artificial, digital or toxic. A green cast is the classic shorthand for a simulated or sickly world.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Use Duv Tint toward green for fluorescent-lit interiors and digital-world looks. For natural landscapes, pull foliage toward yellow-green with Hue vs Hue and lower its saturation slightly so skin stays dominant.

colorPsychology.name: Cyan / Teal

culturalMeanings.meaning: turquoise as protection and good fortune

colorPsychology.cinematicUse: The shadow half of the teal and orange look. Opposite skin on the wheel, so it makes faces pop without touching them.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Aim the Lift wheel at teal (around 180-195 degrees) at low strength. Increase separation by shifting background greens toward teal with Hue vs Hue instead of tinting the whole frame.

colorPsychology.name: Blue
colorPsychology.cinematicUse: Cinema shorthand for night, moonlight, loneliness and technology. Blue is physically the hardest hue to expose cleanly in low light, so it often carries noise.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: For day-for-night, drop exposure 2-3 stops, push Kelvin to roughly 4300-4800 K and add blue to Lift and Gamma, then desaturate the warm highlights. Protect skin with a vector qualifier.

colorPsychology.name: Purple / Violet
colorPsychology.cinematicUse: Used for twilight, neon cities and otherworldly scenes. Magenta-purple adds energy; blue-purple adds mystery.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Push Gain highlights toward magenta and Lift toward blue-violet for dusk or neon looks. Many cameras clip purple and blue-violet LEDs, so keep saturation moderate and check the vectorscope.

colorPsychology.name: Pink

culturalMeanings.meaning: a recent, culturally specific association rather than a universal one

colorPsychology.cinematicUse: Soft pinks create warm, dreamy or nostalgic moods. Hot pink and magenta read as neon, energy and rebellion.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Lift blacks slightly toward warm pink for a faded, romantic look. Be careful with skin: heavy pink in the midtones shifts faces off the skin-tone line toward magenta.

colorPsychology.name: Brown

culturalMeanings.meaning: seen as humble and grounded; association with mourning in some regions

colorPsychology.cinematicUse: A dark, desaturated orange. Sepia and amber tones come from here and signal age, memory and history.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Push Gamma toward warm orange, reduce overall saturation by 10-25%, and lift blacks slightly for a vintage or archival feel. Keep highlights neutral so the frame does not look muddy.

colorPsychology.name: Black
colorPsychology.cinematicUse: Deep, controlled blacks create contrast and mood. Crushing blacks hides detail and can add menace; lifting them gives a filmic, faded look.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Set black point near 0-2% for clean contrast; lift to 4-8% for a matte look. Add a slight blue or green into Lift for cooler, more cinematic shadows instead of pure neutral black.

colorPsychology.name: White
colorPsychology.cinematicUse: High-key white feels clean, ethereal or clinical. Overexposed white reads as heaven, memory or amnesia; blue-tinted white reads as cold and sterile.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Keep white at about 90-95% rather than clipping at 100% unless you want a blown-out dream look. Tint highlights slightly warm for friendly scenes, or slightly cool for clinical ones.

colorPsychology.name: Gray
colorPsychology.cinematicUse: Desaturated, gray palettes communicate hardship, bureaucracy or emotional numbness. Neutral gray is also the reference point for balancing everything else.
colorPsychology.gradingTips: Use global saturation at 50-70% with slightly raised contrast for a bleach-bypass feel. Retain a little color in skin so the actors do not look lifeless.

emotionPalettes.description: Cold, low-key and desaturated with one sharp warm accent.
Warm, soft contrast with gentle pinks and golden highlights.
Faded warmth with lifted blacks and muted greens.
Cool, muted blues and grays with low saturation.
Saturated warm primaries with strong punchy contrast.
Gentle cool greens and blues with soft highlights.
Deep violets and teals with controlled, dark shadows.
Warm golden light with clean whites and fresh greens.
Dark, rich tones with metallic gold and deep purples.
Greenish-yellow cast with flat contrast and desaturated skin.

filmStocks.name: Kodak Vision3 50D (5203)
filmStocks.character: Extremely fine grain, clean and neutral with excellent highlight latitude. The sharpest, most detailed of the Vision3 family.
filmStocks.availabilityNote: Current Kodak motion picture catalog stock.

filmStocks.name: Kodak Vision3 250D (5207)
filmStocks.character: Versatile daylight workhorse with natural color, smooth skin and good low-light flexibility. Slightly richer than 50D.
filmStocks.shadowTint: neutral with a hint of warmth
filmStocks.availabilityNote: Current Kodak motion picture catalog stock.

filmStocks.name: Kodak Vision3 200T (5213)
filmStocks.character: Tungsten-balanced, clean and fine-grained, good for controlled interior lighting. Shot in daylight without a filter it shifts blue.
filmStocks.availabilityNote: Current Kodak motion picture catalog stock.

filmStocks.name: Kodak Vision3 500T (5219)
filmStocks.character: The modern low-light standard: rich color, visible but pleasing grain, wide latitude and strong shadow detail. Widely associated with the contemporary "film look".
filmStocks.availabilityNote: Current Kodak motion picture catalog stock.

filmStocks.name: Kodak Portra 160
filmStocks.character: Soft, pastel contrast with extremely smooth skin and subtle, muted color. Very forgiving with overexposure.

filmStocks.name: Kodak Portra 400
filmStocks.character: The all-round portrait film: warm skin, gentle contrast, subtle pastel color and a clean, slightly pushed-red feel.
filmStocks.shadowTint: neutral with a touch of warm brown
filmStocks.skinRendering: warm and natural, a signature look

filmStocks.name: Kodak Portra 800
filmStocks.character: Same Portra color science with more grain, intended for dim light, events and low-light portraiture.
filmStocks.skinRendering: warm and soft with visible grain

filmStocks.name: Kodak Ektar 100
filmStocks.character: Very saturated, very fine-grained negative film with punchy reds and rich blues. Handles skin less gently than Portra.
filmStocks.skinRendering: ruddier and more saturated than Portra

filmStocks.name: Kodak Gold 200
filmStocks.character: Consumer film with warm golden-yellow cast, sunny nostalgia and a slightly saturated, family-photo feel.

filmStocks.name: Kodak Tri-X 400
filmStocks.character: Classic black & white with pronounced grain, rich midtone separation and a gritty documentary feel.

filmStocks.name: Fujifilm Velvia 50
filmStocks.character: The landscape benchmark: hyper-saturated greens, blues and reds with high contrast and very little forgiveness in exposure.
filmStocks.skinRendering: warm and saturated, can look ruddy
filmStocks.availabilityNote: Availability and ISO range vary by region; check with Fujifilm.

filmStocks.name: Fujifilm Provia 100F
filmStocks.character: Neutral, accurate slide film with moderate saturation and fine grain. A general-purpose reference-style look.

filmStocks.name: Fujifilm Pro 400H
filmStocks.character: Pastel, airy look with cool-leaning greens and soft, creamy skin. A favorite for bright, high-key wedding and fashion work.
filmStocks.availabilityNote: Discontinued by Fujifilm; available only as leftover stock or through emulations.

filmStocks.name: Fujifilm Superia X-Tra 400
filmStocks.character: Everyday consumer film with a characteristic green-cyan shadow shift, punchy greens and a snapshot aesthetic.

filmStocks.name: CineStill 800T
filmStocks.character: Motion-picture tungsten film adapted for still cameras. Famous for red halation glow around bright lights and cool teal shadows.
filmStocks.highlightTint: warm with red halation around lights
filmStocks.skinRendering: warm under tungsten, cool-shifted under daylight
filmStocks.availabilityNote: Current CineStill catalog film (based on a motion-picture stock).

filmStocks.name: Ilford HP5 Plus 400
filmStocks.character: Flexible, forgiving black & white film with moderate grain and smooth tonal gradation. Pushes well.
filmStocks.skinRendering: smooth tonal skin rendering in monochrome

lookPresets.name: Day - Natural Neutral
lookPresets.description: Clean daylight rendering with balanced skin, mild S-curve and no color cast.

lookPresets.name: Day - Golden Hour
lookPresets.description: Warm low-angle sun with orange highlights, softened shadows and gentle halo.
cautions: Do not push warm so far that skin loses detail in the red channel.

lookPresets.name: Day - Overcast Soft
lookPresets.description: Muted, low-contrast daylight with a cool-neutral tone and creamy skin.
cautions: Raise midtone contrast slightly to avoid a flat image.

lookPresets.name: Night - Moonlight Blue
lookPresets.description: Cool, low-key moonlit night with desaturated warm accents and deep blue shadows.
cautions: Blue channel noise rises in low light; apply noise reduction before grading.

lookPresets.name: Night - Neon City
lookPresets.description: Magenta and cyan practicals with crushed blacks and glowing highlights.
cautions: Saturated magenta and cyan clip easily; watch vectorscope boundaries.

lookPresets.name: Day-for-Night Lab
lookPresets.description: Converts daylight footage to convincing night: lower exposure, blue shift, crushed warm highlights.
cautions: Shadows from harsh sun give it away; use overcast or backlit plates.
Mask the sky or darken with a gradient.

lookPresets.name: Blue Hour Twilight
lookPresets.description: Deep blue ambient light with warm artificial accents - the in-between hour.
cautions: Balance warm practical lights with a small amount of orange so they do not look cyan.

lookPresets.name: Teal & Orange Blockbuster
lookPresets.description: Cool teal shadows against warm orange skin and highlights - the modern action and sci-fi staple.
cautions: Protect skin with a vector qualifier or Hue vs Hue so faces do not go orange-plastic.
Use moderately; extreme settings reduce natural color variety.

lookPresets.name: Bleach Bypass
lookPresets.description: Desaturated, high-contrast, silvery image with gritty texture and retained highlights.
cautions: Do not desaturate skin fully; it looks lifeless.

lookPresets.name: Film Noir Monochrome
lookPresets.description: High-contrast black and white with deep shadows and sharp, hard-lit highlights.
cautions: Use a channel mixer or color filter (red/orange) to control skin and sky tones in B&W.

lookPresets.name: Digital Green Cast
lookPresets.description: Strong green tint in shadows and midtones for artificial, simulated or toxic worlds.
cautions: Heavy green kills skin plausibility; use it deliberately, not everywhere.

lookPresets.name: Pastel Storybook
lookPresets.description: Lifted blacks, soft pinks and creams, restrained contrast and warm highlights.
cautions: Keep highlight detail; do not wash out entirely.

lookPresets.name: Faded 1970s Film
lookPresets.description: Warm amber cast, faded blacks and lowered saturation, reminiscent of aged color prints.
cautions: Add subtle grain and soft halation to sell the effect.

lookPresets.name: Cold Horror
lookPresets.description: Desaturated, cold, green-blue shadows with a sickly cast and crushed blacks.
cautions: Keep a small warm accent for contrast; entirely cold images feel flat.

lookPresets.name: Atmospheric Depth
lookPresets.description: Lifted, slightly hazy shadows with cooler background and warmer subject to create layered depth.
cautions: Use a power window or depth matte to separate subject from background.

lookPresets.name: Desert Heat
lookPresets.description: Hot yellow-orange sun, bleached highlights and sandy mid-tones.
cautions: Protect skin from turning orange; pull saturation in the red-orange range slightly.

lookPresets.name: Arctic Cold
lookPresets.description: Icy blue-white with low saturation, bright highlights and slightly raised blacks.
cautions: Keep a little warmth in skin or faces will look cyan and unhealthy.

tones.label: Very Fair / Pale
tones.description: Very light skin that burns easily; pink or neutral undertones; visible redness shows quickly.
lightingTips: Use soft diffusion; hard light exaggerates redness and blemishes.
Avoid overexposing: skin clips early in the red channel.
gradingTips: Reduce red saturation slightly with Hue vs Sat to calm ruddiness.
Keep highlights from touching 100% so freckles and texture survive.
commonProblems: pink or magenta cast in shadows

tones.label: Fair / Light
tones.description: Light skin that burns easily and tans minimally; commonly cool or neutral undertones.
lightingTips: Soft frontal light flatters; add a warm kicker to separate from backgrounds.
gradingTips: Align the average skin hue to the skin-tone line, then nudge to taste.
Use a low-saturation qualifier to protect skin during teal & orange grades.
commonProblems: green or yellow cast under fluorescent lights
skin looking waxy when saturation is lowered

tones.label: Medium / Light Olive
tones.description: Light-to-medium skin that tans gradually; warm, neutral or olive undertones.
lightingTips: Works well with both warm and neutral light; watch green spill on olive undertones.
gradingTips: If skin looks greenish, nudge Duv Tint slightly toward magenta (+0.02 to +0.05).
Use Hue vs Hue to pull yellow-green skin toward the skin line.
commonProblems: skin turning orange when grading warm

tones.label: Tan / Moderate Brown
tones.description: Moderate brown skin that tans easily; commonly warm golden or olive undertones.
lightingTips: Use a slightly larger source and enough fill that facial structure stays readable.
gradingTips: Lift skin midtones slightly rather than raising global exposure.
Avoid heavy orange tints; they flatten tonal variation.
commonProblems: orange or muddy skin when over-warmed

tones.label: Brown / Deep
tones.description: Deep brown skin that rarely burns; range of warm red-brown to neutral and cool undertones.
lightingTips: Use specular highlights (soft kickers or rim light) to shape the face and reveal texture.
Expose for skin, not for the background; underexposure introduces noise and a gray veil.
gradingTips: Avoid pulling blacks up on dark skin; it creates a washed-out, gray look.
Add a modest midtone contrast curve to keep highlights luminous.

tones.label: Very Deep / Dark Brown
tones.description: Very deep brown to blue-black skin that does not burn; strong reflective highlights.
lightingTips: Ensure enough light on the face so detail does not fall into the noise floor.
Shape with contrast and specular glow instead of flat fill.
gradingTips: Protect skin from teal shadow tinting; it can turn skin ashy.
Use a power window with soft edges to brighten faces gently without lifting the whole frame.
commonProblems: inconsistent exposure vs lighter-skinned cast members

gradingRules: Skin of all complexions clusters along a narrow hue band; the exposure and saturation change far more than the hue.
Balance white or gray objects first, then adjust skin by eye so the grade does not depend on skin alone.
Use a qualifier or Hue vs Hue to isolate skin before applying strong stylistic color shifts.
Check the vectorscope: skin samples should cluster near the skin-tone line, not scatter across the dial.
Match skin across shots in a scene before applying the creative look.
Do not rely on a single average value: shadows, midtones and highlights of skin shift slightly in hue.
View the image on a calibrated display; skin errors are the first thing audiences notice.

schemes.name: Monochromatic
schemes.description: A single hue in varying lightness and saturation.
schemes.cinematicUse: Dream sequences, stylized worlds, and strong single-mood scenes.
usageTips: Vary lightness and saturation for depth; the image will look flat without tonal range.
Add a tiny hue shift between shadows and highlights to avoid a single-tint look.

schemes.name: Analogous
schemes.description: Three neighboring hues on the color wheel.
schemes.cinematicUse: Natural landscapes, sunsets, period dramas, and quiet interiors.
usageTips: Pick one dominant hue; let the others support it.
Add a small complementary accent to avoid dullness.

schemes.name: Complementary
schemes.description: Two hues opposite each other on the wheel.
schemes.cinematicUse: Teal and orange, blue and amber, red and cyan - skin versus background separation.
usageTips: Use one color as dominant (about 70-80%) and the other as accent.
Desaturate one of them for a more sophisticated look.

schemes.name: Split-Complementary
schemes.description: A base hue plus the two hues adjacent to its complement.
schemes.mood: contrasty but less tense than a pure complement
schemes.cinematicUse: Character-driven scenes where you want contrast without a stark clash.
usageTips: Great for beginners: strong contrast with easier balance.
Let the base hue dominate and use the others as accents.

schemes.name: Triadic
schemes.description: Three hues evenly spaced around the wheel.
schemes.cinematicUse: Comic-book looks, children's stories, and heightened-reality worlds.
usageTips: One hue should dominate; keep the others muted.
Lower saturation in two of the three for a grown-up palette.

schemes.name: Tetradic (Rectangle)
schemes.description: Two complementary pairs forming a rectangle on the wheel.
schemes.cinematicUse: Production design and costume palettes with a lot of variety.
usageTips: Pick a dominant pair and treat the other as accents.
Control saturation or the image can feel chaotic.

schemes.name: Square
schemes.description: Four hues evenly spaced at 90-degree intervals.
schemes.cinematicUse: Highly stylized pop worlds and music videos.
usageTips: Use one hue as the lead and keep the rest low saturation.
Works best with strong neutral anchors (black, white, gray).

schemes.name: Double Split-Complementary
schemes.description: Two analogous pairs, each opposite the other.
schemes.cinematicUse: Complex worlds that need color variety without clashing.
usageTips: Treat it like two analogous groups; make one group clearly dominant.

schemes.name: Compound / Accented Analogous
schemes.description: An analogous group plus the complement of its center hue.
schemes.cinematicUse: Sunset scenes with a cool accent, or cool nights with a warm practical.
usageTips: The complement should cover a small area, such as a light source or a costume detail.

schemes.name: Neutral + Single Accent
schemes.description: A neutral or desaturated frame with one saturated accent.
schemes.cinematicUse: A red coat in a gray city, a yellow cab in a blue street, or a single colored light source.
usageTips: Keep the accent to under about 10% of the frame.

pipelines.name: Log to Rec.709 with CST (Manual Color Managed)
pipelines.summary: A clean, controllable node tree: convert camera log into a working space, grade there, then convert to Rec.709 for delivery.
bestFor: ARRI LogC, Sony S-Log3, Canon C-Log, RED Log3G10, Panasonic V-Log

colorManagement.mode: DaVinci YRGB (not Color Managed) with manual CST nodes
colorManagement.inputColorSpace: Camera log (e.g. ARRI LogC3 / Sony S-Log3 S-Gamut3.Cine)

nodes.label: Noise Reduction (optional)
nodes.purpose: Clean up before any contrast or saturation work so noise is not amplified.
settings: Spatial NR: Mode Faster/Better, light amount

nodes.label: Input CST
nodes.purpose: Convert camera log into DaVinci Wide Gamut / DaVinci Intermediate.
settings: Input Color Space: your camera gamut
Input Gamma: your camera log curve
Output Color Space: DaVinci Wide Gamut
Tone Mapping: None (or Luminance Mapping if needed)
Gamut Mapping: Saturation Compression for extreme gamuts
nodes.watchFor: Wrong input settings are the most common cause of a bad base look.

nodes.label: Exposure / Balance
nodes.purpose: Set exposure and neutral white balance on a reference gray or skin.
settings: Use Offset wheel for overall printer-light balance
Check RGB Parade so R/G/B sit level on neutral areas

nodes.label: Contrast & Pivot
nodes.purpose: Establish contrast around a pivot near middle gray.

nodes.label: Skin Tone
nodes.purpose: Isolate skin and place it on the skin-tone line.
settings: HSL qualifier: pick skin; widen Hue slightly and soften with Blur Radius
Use Hue vs Hue to shift skin towards the line
nodes.watchFor: Hard qualifier edges cause visible flicker or noise.

nodes.label: Look: Hue vs Hue / Sat
nodes.purpose: Refine individual color families for the look.
settings: Hue vs Sat: reduce overly saturated greens 10-20%
Hue vs Hue: nudge foliage towards yellow-green or teal as the look requires

nodes.label: Look: Color Warper
nodes.purpose: Apply creative palette shifts with intuitive hue/sat handles.
settings: Move shadow-region hue handles toward teal
Move highlight-region handles toward warm orange

nodes.label: Film Texture
nodes.purpose: Add grain and subtle halation for a filmic finish.
settings: Film Grain: choose a stock preset; keep Strength low (10-25%)
Halation: Threshold high, Radius moderate, red-orange tint
nodes.watchFor: Excess grain on already compressed footage creates mush.

nodes.label: Output CST
nodes.purpose: Convert the working space to Rec.709 for delivery.
settings: Input Color Space: DaVinci Wide Gamut
Tone Mapping: DaVinci / Luminance Mapping for smooth highlight roll-off
nodes.watchFor: Always place the output CST last, after all creative nodes.

tips: Keep technical nodes (CSTs) separated from creative nodes so you can bypass them to debug.
Name each node; a labelled tree is far easier to hand off to another colorist.
Use shot-level nodes for balance and group-level nodes for the look.

pipelines.name: Teal & Orange Split-Tone
pipelines.summary: A modern blockbuster split-tone that keeps skin natural while pushing shadows cool and highlights warm.

colorManagement.mode: Any; works best after a CST into a wide working space
colorManagement.inputColorSpace: Rec.709 or camera log after input CST

nodes.label: Base Balance
nodes.purpose: Neutralize the image first so the split tone is deliberate.
settings: Balance whites and blacks using RGB Parade

nodes.label: Cool Shadows
nodes.purpose: Push shadows toward teal/blue-green.
settings: Shadow wheel: move toward cyan-teal (about 180-200 degrees), small amount
Midtone wheel: tiny push toward blue to extend the cool range

nodes.label: Warm Highlights
nodes.purpose: Push highlights toward warm orange.
settings: Highlight wheel: move toward orange (about 20-35 degrees), small amount

nodes.label: Protect Skin
nodes.purpose: Isolate skin and reduce the teal/orange influence so faces stay natural.
settings: HSL qualifier on skin; invert to affect the background if needed
Use Hue vs Hue to nudge skin onto the skin-tone line
nodes.watchFor: Over-warm skin looks orange or plastic.

nodes.label: Background Teal Boost
nodes.purpose: Shift greens and blues toward teal for separation.
settings: Hue vs Hue: move green toward teal by 10-20 percent
Hue vs Sat: lower saturation of competing greens

nodes.label: Contrast Curve
nodes.purpose: Add a gentle S-curve to finish the look.
settings: Custom curve: lower shadows slightly, raise highlights slightly

tips: Strength matters more than direction: subtle looks age better than extreme ones.
Check the vectorscope: skin should stay near the skin line while shadows lean cyan and highlights lean orange.

pipelines.name: Day-for-Night
pipelines.summary: Turn daylight footage into believable night using exposure, color temperature and masking.

colorManagement.inputColorSpace: Rec.709 or camera log after input CST

nodes.label: Base Balance
nodes.purpose: Clean neutral balance before the night look.
settings: Balance whites using the RGB Parade

nodes.label: Exposure Down
nodes.purpose: Reduce exposure by 2-3 stops equivalent.
settings: Gamma down slightly; protect a little shadow detail

nodes.label: Blue Shift
nodes.purpose: Move overall color temperature toward moonlight blue.
settings: Shadows and midtones toward blue; keep skin from going gray

nodes.label: Desaturate
nodes.purpose: Night reduces color perception; lower saturation 25-40%.
settings: Keep a small amount of warm color in practical lights

nodes.label: Sky Control
nodes.purpose: Darken the sky with a gradient so it does not read as daytime.
settings: Linear window with soft edge from top of frame
Lower exposure strongly in the sky region
nodes.watchFor: Hard daylight shadows and a bright sky are the biggest tells.

nodes.label: Highlight Control
nodes.purpose: Pull down bright surfaces so they do not look sun-lit.
settings: Luma qualifier on highlights; reduce gain and add blue

nodes.label: Practical Lights
nodes.purpose: Add warmth and glow to lamps or windows to sell the night.
settings: Qualify bright lights; push warm orange and add Glow

tips: Overcast or backlit footage converts much more convincingly than frontal sunlight.
Lift contrast in the highlights slightly so lights glow against the darker frame.

pipelines.name: Bleach Bypass Look
pipelines.summary: High-contrast, desaturated, silvery look with retained highlights.

nodes.label: Base Balance
nodes.purpose: Neutral starting point.

nodes.label: Desaturated Copy
nodes.purpose: Create a desaturated layer for blending.
settings: Set Saturation to 0 on a parallel/layer node

nodes.label: Contrast Boost
nodes.purpose: Strong S-curve on the desaturated layer.
settings: Set the layer Key Output around 0.4-0.6 to blend
nodes.watchFor: Pushing blacks too hard crushes detail.

nodes.label: Skin Recovery
nodes.purpose: Bring back some color in skin so faces are not dead.
settings: HSL qualifier on skin; restore saturation 20-35%

tips: Add subtle grain to sell a photochemical feel.

toolGuides.whatItDoes: Rotates selected hues toward other hues.
toolGuides.whenToUse: Shift foliage toward yellow or teal, move skin onto the skin-tone line, fix off-color brand items.
tips: Use soft curves with wide support points to avoid banding.
Always sample the target color with the picker.

toolGuides.whatItDoes: Raises or lowers saturation for a selected hue.
toolGuides.whenToUse: Tame oversaturated greens or reds, boost blues in skies, and refine a limited palette.
tips: Pull rather than push; subtle edits look more natural.

toolGuides.whatItDoes: Changes brightness for a selected hue.
toolGuides.whenToUse: Darken blue skies, brighten skin, or lift foliage without touching the rest of the frame.
tips: Check noise in the blue channel when darkening skies.

toolGuides.whatItDoes: Hue/Sat and Chroma/Luma grid for bending color regions with direct handles.
toolGuides.whenToUse: Fast creative palette work and complex color relationships.
tips: Lock handles around skin before moving neighbours.
Use Chroma-Luma mode to adjust saturation by brightness.

toolGuides.whatItDoes: Color Space Transform: converts between color spaces and gamma curves with tone and gamut mapping.
toolGuides.whenToUse: Move footage between camera log and a working or delivery space.
tips: Match input settings exactly to the camera.
Put the output CST at the end of the node tree.

toolGuides.whatItDoes: Selects a range of hue, saturation and luminance.
toolGuides.whenToUse: Skin, sky, foliage and highlight control.
tips: Soften the matte with Blur Radius and Denoise.
View the matte with Highlight (Shift+H) to check it.

recipes.name: Cinematic Teal & Orange
recipes.summary: Warm skin and highlights against cool teal shadows and backgrounds, using Color Grading and HSL.

steps.goal: Set a clean, slightly flat base.
Steer colors toward teal and orange.
settings: Green: Hue toward teal (+20 to +40), Saturation -20 to -40
steps.watchFor: Moving Orange hue or saturation too far will tint skin unnaturally.

steps.goal: Create split-toning between shadows and highlights.
settings: Blending 50-60, Balance slightly toward shadows (-10 to -20)

steps.goal: Fine-tune the primaries for a deeper, more filmic palette.
settings: Red Primary: Hue +5 to +15, Saturation -5 to -10
Green Primary: Hue +10 to +20, Saturation -10 to -20
Blue Primary: Hue -10 to -20, Saturation +10 to +20
Shadows Tint: +5 to +10 toward green or -5 to -10 toward magenta as needed
steps.watchFor: Calibration changes affect every color; small adjustments go a long way.

steps.goal: Add a subtle grain and vignette.

tips: Use Masking > Subject to protect skin from background teal shifts.
Compare before and after at 100% to check skin and noise.

recipes.name: HSL Depth: Moody Landscape
recipes.summary: Use HSL luminance to carve depth: darken skies and foliage, brighten key subjects.

steps.watchFor: Darkening blue too much can introduce noise and banding in skies.

steps.goal: Add a subtle cool-to-warm tonal contrast.
Use gradients and subject masks for depth.

exportFormats.name: 3D LUT (Cube)
exportFormats.description: Text-based 3D lookup table: a grid of RGB output values for sampled RGB inputs.
notes: Common sizes: 17, 33 and 65 points per axis. 33 is a good default.
Declare input range with DOMAIN_MIN/DOMAIN_MAX and size with LUT_3D_SIZE.
Cube data is ordered with red changing fastest, then green, then blue.
A LUT built for Rec.709 will not give correct results on log footage unless you convert first.

exportFormats.name: Adobe Swatch Exchange
exportFormats.description: Binary swatch format for sharing named color palettes across Adobe apps.
notes: Store each swatch with a name and RGB or CMYK values.
Keep names descriptive, such as "Teal Shadow 190".

exportFormats.name: Lightroom / Camera Raw Preset
exportFormats.description: XML preset that stores develop settings (crs: keys) for Lightroom Classic and Adobe Camera Raw.
notes: Test exported presets on a real image after any change to the key map.
Color Grading keys require a recent Lightroom version; split-toning keys cover older versions.

exportFormats.name: PDF Lookbook
exportFormats.description: A shareable document with swatches, grade values and reference notes for clients and crew.
notes: Include hex values and wheel settings so a colorist can recreate the look.
